column1: # The framebuffer scene for decision 0007 task 5, bullet 2.
# Tab-separated. The first column is the record kind.
#   frame   width height viewwindowx viewwindowy centery
#           The geometry every job is drawn into. `centery` is passed rather
#           than derived: the original derives it once, in `initialize`.
#           THE TWO WINDOW ORIGINS DIFFER FROM EACH OTHER on purpose. They are
#           separate parameters reaching the kernel in separate positions, and
#           while they held the same number a caller or a generator that
#           swapped them drew exactly the same screen -- a whole class of
#           defect that nothing here could see. Measured: with both at 4 the
#           swap passed every lane in every capability; with 6 and 4 it fails
#           them. The check rows below are placed against x + viewwindowx,
#           so they moved with it.
#   seed    the seed of the generator that fills the screen and the resources
#   res     name bytes -- how big each resource is. `atlas` is a whole number
#           of 128-byte texture columns and `flat` of 4096-byte flats, which
#           is what the job banks' `srcofs` fields are declared to be multiples
#           of; `cmap` is 34 rows of 256. There are TWO flats, so a span whose
#           `srcofs` selected the wrong one draws the wrong bytes; with one
#           flat, `srcofs` could only ever be zero and dropping it would be
#           invisible.
#   job     kind and seven fields, IN THE BANK'S FIELD ORDER, so a row here
#           reads the same way as a row of Doom::Jobs:
#             wall  x  yl yh iscale   texmid srcofs cmap
#             span  y  x1 x2 position step   srcofs cmap
#             fuzz  x  yl yh fz       -      -      -
#           The rows are THE SCHEDULE: they are executed top to bottom, and
#           that order is part of the answer.
#   check   kind, seven fields, the status the CORE kernel must return, and
#           why. These are NOT part of the schedule and are NOT run through
#           CRuby, because they are where CRuby and the CORE ABI part company.
#           See "What CRuby cannot answer for" below.
# WHY THESE JOBS. Job 4 is a fuzz column over the wall drawn by job 1 and the
# span drawn by job 2, so it reads pixels those two wrote -- that is the
# neighbouring access. Job 7 is a fuzz column whose starting phase is 47, so
# its `fp` wraps through 50 back to 0 while it draws. Job 16 redraws part of
# the column job 4 fuzzed, so running the schedule in any other order gives a
# different screen, which is what makes the order check non-vacuous.
# The spans are chosen so that every term of `spot = (position >> 26) |
# ((position >> 4) & 0x0fc0)` actually moves. `step` 8389632 is 0x00800400:
# bit 10 carries into the second term every pixel and bit 23 into the first
# every eighth, so a span that lost either term draws different bytes for
# most of its length. Jobs 10 and 11 read the SECOND flat, so `srcofs` is a
# choice and not a constant zero.
# Empty and single-element work is in the schedule by design rather than by
# accident: jobs 8, 9 and 15 have yh < yl or x2 < x1 and must draw
# nothing, and jobs 10, 12 and 14 are a one-pixel span, column and fuzz
# column. Without those, a kernel whose emptiness guard was off by one
# would draw the same screen as one whose guard was right.
# WHAT CRUBY CANNOT ANSWER FOR. Two things, and the `check` rows carry both.
#   Indices off the end. A Ruby Array reads nil or grows; the CORE ABI
#   answers SPINEL_CORE_BOUNDS (3). Every declared buffer face of every
#   kernel has a pair here -- the screen (written, and read by fuzz above and
#   below), the atlas, the flat atlas, the colormap from both the wall and
#   the span, and the fuzz table -- and each pair is the exact last index and
#   the one after it, so an `index <= count` off-by-one fails one of them.
#   i64 arithmetic. CRuby integers are arbitrary precision, so the ORIGINAL
#   draws for every `texmid`; the CORE kernel computes in i64 and answers
#   SPINEL_CORE_ARITHMETIC (2) when `texmid + (yl - centery) * iscale`
#   overflows. THIS IS A REAL FULL/CORE DIVERGENCE and the pair below pins
#   exactly where it starts: with yl 0 and centery 20 the addend is -1310720,
#   so texmid -9223372036853465088 is the last value both agree on.
# Status 1 (ARGUMENT) and 4 (CAPACITY) do not appear and cannot: ARGUMENT is
# about the pointers and counts the harness passes, which tests/core-boundary/
# buffers.sh covers, and none of these kernels calls core_fail(:capacity).
# The divergence does not run only one way. The ORIGINAL has no guard of its
# own for a `fz` outside the fuzz table: `@fuzzoffset[fz]` is nil and
# exec_masked dies with `undefined method '*' for nil`, where the kernel
# answers SPINEL_CORE_BOUNDS. So "the original draws wherever the kernel
# refuses" is true of the arithmetic edge and false of the table edge, and
# neither is a claim this scene makes in general.
# WHAT THE CHECKS CANNOT SEE. The kernels address the screen as one linear
# buffer, which is what the ABI declares, so the boundary they enforce is
# that buffer's end and not the right-hand edge of the picture. A column at
# x = 70 on a 64-wide screen writes into the next row and is accepted; only
# running off the buffer is SPINEL_CORE_BOUNDS. Keeping x below the width
# stays the caller's obligation, exactly as it is in R_DrawColumn.
